Detroit by the numbers

Which office bills Detroit homeowners?

The City of Detroit bills its own property tax through the Office of the Treasury, and the Wayne County Treasurer takes over once a bill goes delinquent. The Office of the Assessor sets the values. Use the due dates printed on your Detroit bill, and ask the Office of the Treasury if a date is unclear.

Wayne County's treasurer states the handoff rule plainly: any bill still open with the city after the end of February turns delinquent on March 1, and from that day only the county accepts payment. Detroit joined the county's Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund program with tax year 2003, under Public Act 246.

What happens when Detroit property tax goes unpaid?

A Detroit parcel can go from delinquent to foreclosed in about two years, and the interest climbs at each step. Wayne County's treasurer describes the sequence this way.

Delinquent tax stages for Detroit parcels, per the Wayne County Treasurer
StageTimingWhat changes
DelinquentMarch 1 after the tax yearPayable only to Wayne County; interest at 1% a month
ForfeitedThe next March 1Interest becomes 1.5% a month, back to the original delinquency date, plus a $175 foreclosure fee and $30 in recording fees
ForeclosedMarch 31 after a year in forfeiture, in an uncontested caseTitle goes to the Wayne County Treasurer and a judgment is recorded
AuctionSeptember and October of that yearMinimum bid equals taxes, penalties, interest and costs

The office sends at least ten written notices before foreclosure, four during the first year of delinquency and six after forfeiture. A foreclosed parcel is first offered to the state, the city, the county or an authority at the minimum bid, and anything left goes to the September and October auctions, where winning bidders receive a quit claim deed. The county also says it cannot waive penalties and interest on a current bill.

What help exists for Detroit owners behind on tax?

Wayne County runs payment plans for owners who occupy their homes and face financial hardship. The county's income standard is 125% of the federal poverty level, and applicants with income just above that line are told to apply anyway. Staff review the file and reply within 30 days of receiving it.

  • Applicants need a Michigan driver's license or state ID, a copy of the deed, proof that the home is the principal residence, and proof of income.
  • Owners by recorded deed or land contract can qualify.
  • The Poverty Tax Exemption comes from the local assessing unit, so Detroit residents ask the city's assessor, not the county.
  • Calls to the treasurer's taxpayer assistance line go to (313) 224-5990, and email goes to taxinfo@waynecountymi.gov.
  • The same office can send text reminders about plan payments, which you can request by phone or email.
  • A hardship extension that was granted and paid off in an earlier year does not bar a new application if hardship continues.

When the owner has died and the house is still in a relative's name, the treasurer points families to Lakeshore Legal Aid at 888-783-8190 and the Wayne County Probate Court at 313-224-5706. For title help, the county's FAQ lists United Community Housing Coalition at (313) 963-3310 and Legal Aid and Defender at (313) 964-4130.

Where does a Detroit assessment appeal begin?

Detroit assessment appeals start with the city's Board of Review and can continue to the Michigan Tax Tribunal, the two bodies that Wayne County's treasurer names as able to change a tax figure. The county treasurer cannot reduce a bill once it is issued.

Ask the Office of the Assessor for the current filing window and forms, because the dates change by year.

How do Detroit size and layout affect a seller?

Detroit covers 142.87 square miles, of which 138.75 are land, along the Detroit River in the southeast corner of Michigan. The ground slopes gently from the northwest toward the river on a clay till plain, and the French established Fort Pontchartrain du Detroit on July 24, 1701. The climate is hot-summer humid continental, with temperatures staying below freezing on about 44 days a year.

Neighborhoods vary a great deal. Downtown, Midtown, Corktown and New Center are dense and historic, Lafayette Park is a Mies van der Rohe district, and southwest Detroit has seen new housing and business openings. Meanwhile, parts of the northeast and the city's fringes have large numbers of vacant lots. Because the city is so large, a single price is a poor guide: compare your own block.

The employment base is automotive, finance, technology and health care. Midtown's Detroit Medical Center is the largest single employer, and General Motors, Rocket Mortgage, Ally Financial and DTE Energy are among the companies headquartered in the city. The Detroit Department of Transportation runs buses within city limits, SMART connects the suburbs, and the QLINE streetcar runs along the central corridor. Four border crossings link the city to Windsor, and the Gordie Howe International Bridge is listed as opened in 2026.

How do Detroit housing numbers compare?

QuickFacts shows a city whose figures sit far from its suburbs'. The July 2025 estimate for Detroit is 649,095 people, a gain of 1.5% since the 2020 census base.

  • Owner-held houses carry a median value of $83,900 for 2020-2024, against $354,500 in Farmington Hills.
  • Owners occupy 50.3% of housing, across 257,998 households.
  • Households have a median income of $39,938, and 32.7% of people fall below the poverty line.
  • Renters pay a median of $1,074 a month.

Where values run this low, an overdue balance of a few thousand dollars can take a big bite out of a sale price. Request the exact payoff early.

How is the tax balance cleared at a Detroit closing?

Under MCL 211.135 a register of deeds asks for treasurer certificates covering tax liens and a five-year tax history before a deed is recorded. A warranty deed can be refused until they are in the file. Quitclaim deeds and some other conveyances are excepted.

Deed certification happens at Wayne County's Treasurer's Office, 400 Monroe Street, 5th Floor, Detroit, MI 48226, for $5 a document with up to 25 parcel numbers and 20 cents for each parcel beyond that. Only originals qualify, never copies. The certified deed then moves on to the county's recording office, which needs its own appointment.

Delinquent payments by bank transfer online cost nothing, while cards add 2.49%, which goes to the service provider. Wayne County warns that its staff never come to a home to collect money, so pay only at the office, online, at an authorized kiosk or by mail.

More questions about Detroit, MI Property Tax Guide

Who takes payment on delinquent Detroit property tax?

The Wayne County Treasurer. Unpaid bills turn delinquent on March 1 and are payable only to the county from then on. The office is at 400 Monroe Street, 5th Floor, Detroit, and takes calls at (313) 224-5990.

How fast can Detroit tax foreclosure happen?

Roughly two years. A parcel forfeits on the March 1 after delinquency begins, then can be foreclosed the following March 31 in an uncontested case, with auctions in September and October.

What interest applies to delinquent Detroit property tax?

Interest runs 1% a month at first, then 1.5% a month once the parcel is forfeited, applied back to the date the tax became delinquent. A $175 fee and $30 recording fee are added at forfeiture.

Can a Detroit house with back taxes be sold?

Yes. Proceeds cover the balance at the closing table, and the title company relies on the treasurer's certification. Ask Wayne County for a written payoff first, because interest keeps adding up.

Does Detroit offer relief from property tax?

Possibly. Wayne County runs payment plans for owner-occupants, and the Poverty Tax Exemption is requested through the city's assessing office. Ask the Office of the Assessor for the current application.

Ann Arbor by the numbers

Which city office issues an Ann Arbor tax bill?

Ann Arbor collects its own property tax through the Treasury unit, and the city's Assessor sets the values behind each bill. Once real property tax stays unpaid past winter, the account moves to Washtenaw County.

The city's Assessing page reports that over half of Ann Arbor's revenue comes from property tax, so assessments draw close scrutiny. A bill is a combined figure: the city levy, plus the county, the schools and other taxing units, each setting its own millage.

A separate administration fee also appears. State law lets the city add up to 1 percent of the tax, and the money offsets the work of defending assessments and collecting for every taxing unit.

What dates matter on the Ann Arbor tax calendar?

Two bills arrive each year: summer tax is billed July 1 and winter tax December 1, with the last penalty-free days at the end of those months. County operating tax rides on the summer bill, and the voted county millages ride on the winter one.

Missing the winter deadline starts a short countdown. Real property tax still unpaid on February 28 is passed to the Washtenaw County Treasurer, and extra penalties and interest begin March 1. The city's online record stops at that handoff, so confirm with the county whether a late balance has been paid.

Key dates and payment points listed by the City of Ann Arbor Treasury
ItemDetail
Summer taxPayable from July 1, due July 31
Winter taxPayable from December 1, due December 31
Real property turned over to the countyAfter February 28 following the tax year
Summer deferment filing deadlineSeptember 15

Pay by mailCity of Ann Arbor Treasurer, P.O. Box 77602, Detroit, MI 48277-0602

How are Ann Arbor property taxes calculated?

Take the taxable value, divide by 1,000, multiply by the millage rate, then multiply by 1.01 for the fee. Taxable value often trails assessed value because Proposal A, passed by Michigan voters in 1994, ties its yearly growth to the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, with additions counted separately. Assessed value itself targets half of market value.

The city's estimator page shows annual millage totals of 52.8802 for principal residences and 68.8196 for other property. Run purely as arithmetic, a $200,000 taxable value at the first total comes to $10,681.80 with the fee included. Rates move from year to year, and your parcel's real bill follows the units that cover it.

Your taxable value is printed on the annual bill and on the assessment notice, which the city mails around the first week of March. The online property record card holds the figures behind both.

Why does an Ann Arbor tax bill jump after a sale?

Following a sale or transfer, the next tax year's taxable value is set equal to the assessed value, the half-of-market figure. Ann Arbor calls that uncapping. The yearly limit then applies again until ownership changes once more.

That rule is why a buyer's first full bill can top the one you paid. A long-held house may carry a taxable value well under its assessed value, and the buyer begins without that cushion. With homes valued at a median of $453,400, the difference can be sizable.

The Assessor's Office, on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, takes the Property Transfer Affidavit, the Principal Residence Exemption affidavit and the request to rescind that exemption. Hand them in, submit them on the online forms page or mail them. Ask questions at 734.794.6530 or assessor@a2gov.org.

How does a homeowner challenge an Ann Arbor assessment?

Start with the city Board of Review, which sits four days beginning the Monday of March's third week. You appear by appointment, and the Assessor hands out the appeal forms. Board members are appointed citizens, approved by council, and do not work for the city.

The case that works shows assessed value running past 50 percent of true cash value. Objecting that taxes keep climbing does not count, the city explains, because taxable value may rise yearly by inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower. Helpful evidence includes comparable nearby sales, mistakes on your record card and a repair estimate for something like a leaking basement.

  • A homeowner has to protest at the local board before taking a case to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • The Tribunal filing date is July 31 for homes, and May 31 for commercial and industrial real property and business personal property.
  • The board mails its decision some weeks after it adjourns, along with the next appeal steps.

Is a deferment available, and who handles a balance that went delinquent?

Certain owners can put off the summer bill: senior citizens, people with qualifying disabilities or blindness, and eligible servicepersons, veterans and their surviving spouses. A summer deferment carries a $40,000 household income cap. Pick up the application at the Customer Service Center, 301 E. Huron St., or find it at washtenaw.org, and file it with the treasurer by September 15.

Real property balances that moved to the county are handled by the Washtenaw County Treasurer at 734.222.6600 or taxes@washtenaw.org. Overdue personal property tax stays with the city, and 734.994.2833 gives the amount.

If you plan to sell with a bill outstanding, request the figures before you list. The closing agent pays what is owed from your proceeds.

What does an Ann Arbor seller need to know about the city?

Two land speculators founded Ann Arbor in 1824 and named it for their wives, both called Ann, and the bur oaks on the site. The town became the Washtenaw County seat in 1827, a village in 1833 and a city in 1851. The University of Michigan took root there in 1837, and the two grew up together.

The Huron River winds through town, and the Tree Town nickname rests on more than 50,000 street trees. Three freeways ring the city: I-94 on the south and west, US 23 on the east and M-14 on the north. Ann Arbor Public Schools runs the public high schools, among them Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community. The university alone employs about 30,000 workers, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center.

  • Estimated 2025 population: 122,233, down 1.3 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Owners hold 45.5 percent of 50,499 households, which makes renters the majority.
  • Typical home value $453,400, typical gross rent $1,649.
  • Household income at the midpoint: $82,212; adults with a four-year degree or more: 77.9 percent.
  • Monthly owner costs at the midpoint: $2,436 with a mortgage, $1,036 without.

Renters fill more than half of Ann Arbor's homes, so some sellers are landlords or heirs with an older house. When repairs stand in the way of a conventional sale, a buyer who takes the property as-is can close without them.

More questions about Ann Arbor, MI Property Tax Guide

What is the due date for Ann Arbor summer tax?

July 31, with payments accepted from July 1. Winter tax runs on the same pattern, opening December 1 and closing December 31.

Where can I pay my Ann Arbor tax face to face?

Use the Customer Service and Payment Center inside Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A drive-up drop box at East Ann Street and North Fifth Avenue stays open around the clock.

Does selling change an Ann Arbor taxable value?

Yes, for the buyer. The year after a transfer, taxable value is reset to the assessed value, a step the city calls uncapping.

When must an Ann Arbor homeowner file with the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

By July 31, after first protesting at the March Board of Review. Commercial and industrial real property and business personal property must file by May 31.

Who collects Ann Arbor real property tax that is still unpaid in March?

The Washtenaw County Treasurer, at 734.222.6600, takes real property tax not received by February 28. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city.

Grand Rapids ranks second in Michigan by population, with an estimated 201,183 people in 2025 on 44.8 square miles of land. It grew beside the Grand River, where a run of rapids once stopped boats, and its addresses carry NE, NW, SE or SW depending on where they fall relative to Fulton Street and Division Avenue. The city lists 37 neighborhoods, among them Heritage Hill, Eastown, Garfield Park and Alger Heights, and all of them are billed the same way.

What are the Grand Rapids tax due dates and late fees?

The summer bill is due July 31 and the winter bill February 14, each shifting to the following business day when it lands on a weekend. Whatever date applies is printed on your bill.

The two bills do different jobs. Summer carries most of the charges: the City, the Kent Intermediate School District, Grand Rapids Community College, the State of Michigan and the State Education Tax. Winter carries county charges only, at rates set by the Kent County Board of Commissioners.

Grand Rapids tax bills, per the City Treasurer's policy page
BillGoes outDuePenalty after due date
SummerFirst week of JulyJuly 311% of the balance per month
WinterFirst week of DecemberFebruary 144%

A missing bill does not cancel the debt. Phone 616-456-3020 for a copy. The city says it does not report late payments to credit bureaus, yet the penalties still apply.

How does the city turn taxable value into a bill?

Everything starts with taxable value, the number the city taxes, which may equal or fall below assessed value. The assessor revisits market value yearly to set both.

  • PRE percentage: the principal residence exemption excuses 18 school operating mills on the portion of the home that is the owner's residence, so a duplex may be split.
  • Millage: mills per $1,000 of taxable value, with the full rate tied to the school district.
  • Administration: a 1% Property Tax Administration Fee is added.
  • Estimator: an online calculator asks for district, taxable value and PRE.

The city's sample bill assumes a $50,000 taxable value, full PRE and the 2017 millage rate for Grand Rapids schools, and it produces $1,729.07 for summer and winter together. Because that rate is old, use the sample only to follow the arithmetic, and read the current rate on the Kent County website.

Where can a Grand Rapids owner dispute a value?

Start in February at the Assessor's Review by filing a petition with the City Assessor. Unhappy with the answer? Appeal in March to the Board of Review, in writing or by appointment. Only owners who already petitioned the assessor may appear in March.

The July and December boards are narrower. They fix qualified errors the assessor has verified for the current and one earlier year, such as a clerical slip, a mutual mistake of fact or a measuring or math error, and they can grant a poverty exemption for the current year alone. MCL 211.53b is the controlling statute.

Waiting for a board does not suspend payment. After the board's final report reaches the treasurer, a corrected bill follows in roughly 30 days, yet the first bill stays due and penalties keep running. Refunds are paid to whoever paid the tax.

Which Grand Rapids homeowners can delay or reduce a payment?

A deferment moves the summer deadline to the winter deadline. The household must earn under $40,000 and the home must be the owner's principal residence, and the owner must also be in one of these groups:

  • Over age 62
  • Paraplegic or quadriplegic
  • Totally and permanently disabled
  • Blind
  • An eligible veteran, service member, or surviving spouse of one

The city typically grants requests and calls only for missing details. Apply online, print the PDF, or visit the treasurer's office. Exemptions for disabled veterans and for poverty exist too, and the Property Tax Payments and Policies page links the steps.

An owner who cannot clear the whole bill can ask about installments, which add a penalty. Renaissance zone residents may qualify for exemptions annually, but a single late property tax payment anywhere in Michigan disqualifies them.

When must a Grand Rapids owner claim the principal residence exemption?

By June 1, with the City Assessor, using the PRE affidavit. MCL 211.7cc requires a qualified owner who lives in the home as a principal residence and triggers no disqualifying rule.

Missing June 1 can sometimes be repaired. The assessor may ask for proof that the owner lived there on that date and then adjust the current year and as many as three prior years.

What happens in Grand Rapids when taxes go unpaid before a sale?

On March 1 every unpaid real property bill, summer or winter, goes to the Kent County Treasurer, who adds county penalties and a 4% administrative fee. The county can sell parcels more than 24 months delinquent after a court order. Delinquent personal property and most abatement bills stay with the city.

Two checkpoints touch a sale. A recorded warranty deed needs a county treasurer certificate under MCL 211.135 covering the five prior years. The title company also wants a written payoff, which the city treasurer provides for current bills and the Kent County Treasurer for anything past March 1.

An owner facing a balance can list on the market, sell as-is to a cash buyer, or pay it down first. Collect written payoff numbers before choosing a closing date.

What do the Census figures say about housing in Grand Rapids?

QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 shows 80,222 households, a median owner-occupied value of $244,500 and an owner-occupancy rate of 54.0%, below the 65.2% national figure. Median gross rent is $1,266 and median household income is $69,108. About 41.6% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree, and the average commute is 19 minutes.

With nearly half of homes rented, owners of rental parcels should remember that the PRE reaches only the part of a property the owner lives in. The city's Economic Development Department also runs incentive programs for vacant or obsolete property and answers at 616-456-3431.

More questions about Grand Rapids, MI Property Tax Guide

What day is the Grand Rapids summer tax due?

July 31, or the next business day when that is a weekend. Bills go out in the first week of July, and a 1% charge builds for each month the balance sits unpaid.

Who collects Grand Rapids tax after March 1?

The Kent County Treasurer. Unpaid real property bills leave the city on that date, and the county adds penalties and a 4% administrative fee.

Can Grand Rapids homeowners get extra time on the summer bill?

Some can. A household earning under $40,000 that lives in the home may apply for deferment to the winter date if the owner is over 62, disabled, blind, or an eligible veteran or surviving spouse. Installment plans with a penalty are also offered.

When is the Grand Rapids principal residence exemption deadline?

June 1, filed with the City Assessor. A late filing may still be accepted with proof of owner occupancy on that date, reaching the current year and up to three earlier ones.

Does a Board of Review appeal pause a Grand Rapids bill?

No. The original bill stays due. If the board changes the value, the treasurer revises the bill within about 30 days of the final report, and refunds go to whoever paid.

Who bills and collects property tax in Livonia, Michigan?

The City of Livonia assesses and bills its own property tax, and Wayne County steps in only after a bill goes delinquent. The Assessment Department sets values and handles exemption forms. The Treasurer's Office, on the first floor of City Hall at 33000 Civic Center Drive, mails real and personal property tax bills on July 1 and December 1 and collects the payments.

Those payments are split among several taxing bodies listed by the city: the City of Livonia, Livonia Public Schools, Clarenceville Public Schools, Schoolcraft College, the State of Michigan education tax, Wayne County, Wayne County RESA and Oakland ISD. A house in the northeast corner of the city that falls in the Clarenceville district therefore carries a different mix of levies than one in the Livonia Public Schools territory.

  • Treasurer, bills, due dates, deferrals, special assessments, millage questions: (734) 466-2245.
  • Assessment Department, valuation and exemption forms: (734) 466-2220.
  • Water account: (734) 466-2278.
  • Inspection, for outstanding permits, violations, vacant or abandoned property registration fees and certificate of occupancy: (734) 466-2580.

When are Livonia property taxes due?

Summer taxes are billed July 1 and due September 14. Winter taxes are billed December 1 and due February 14. When a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day. Checks go to City of Livonia, Treasurer, 33000 Civic Center Drive, Livonia, MI 48154.

The city says printouts or screenshots from its online system do not count as an original tax bill. A title company closing a Livonia sale should bring the original, or the $5 fee applies. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city treasurer, while delinquent real property tax moves to the county.

How can I look up a Livonia tax bill and special assessments?

The city runs an online property inquiry system at livoniatax.org, using BS&A software. Agree to the disclaimer, search by address, and enter only the street name without Road, Street or Avenue, or just the house number. Click the property, open the Tax Information tab, and the taxes appear by year and season, with a detailed breakdown behind each year.

The city warns that errors on the site do not cancel taxes or special assessments owed, that the official records at City Hall cover current-year collections only, and that payments on delinquent taxes do not show online. To check a delinquent balance, contact the Wayne County Treasurer.

Special assessments are a separate item. Email specials@livonia.gov to request the status on a parcel. Vacant and abandoned property fees, permit issues and violations do not appear in the online system, so a seller who wants a clean closing should ask Inspection for those directly.

What exemptions and deferrals apply to a Livonia home?

The Assessment Department reminds homeowners of the principal residence exemption deadlines. An affidavit filed on or before June 1 earns the exemption on that year's summer and winter levy and later years while the home remains the owner's principal residence. One filed after June 1 and on or before November 1 applies to the current winter levy and later levies.

The city also publishes a form letting a homeowner defer the due date of winter taxes on a principal residence without penalty or interest, for a stated period set each year. Ask the Treasurer's Office which year's form and deadline applies. Wayne County adds that the poverty exemption is reached through the local assessing unit, so Livonia owners facing hardship should start with the Assessment Department, not the county.

Religious, charitable and educational exemption forms, plus personal property forms, are on the Assessment Department page, which accepts forms by email, mail or the City Hall drop box on the east side of the building.

What happens if Livonia property taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid summer and winter bills are forwarded to the Wayne County Treasurer. Wayne County lays out the state timeline this way: on March 1 unpaid taxes become delinquent at the county, adding a 4 percent administration fee and 1 percent interest per month. A $15 collection fee follows on October 1. The next March 1 the parcel forfeits to the county treasurer, with a $175 fee and recording fees, and interest rises to 1.5 percent per month retroactive to the first delinquency.

Foreclosure follows. Michigan's three-year process ends with the circuit court entering a judgment, and unpaid taxes on March 31 of the third year mean the owner loses the property. Wayne County sends at least ten notices before that point.

Owners with a financial hardship can apply for a Wayne County payment plan. Standards cited are 125 percent of the federal poverty level, and the application needs photo ID, a copy of the deed, proof of occupancy and proof of income. After a foreclosure, the former owner can claim remaining auction proceeds by filing a notice of intent by July 1 of that year.

What does it mean to sell a house in Livonia with tax due?

Livonia is a Wayne County city of about 95,500 people at the 2020 census, set roughly 20 miles northwest of downtown Detroit. It covers about 35.7 square miles of land, was organized as Livonia Township in 1835 and became a city in 1950. More than 40,000 housing units were counted in 2020, and only 2.7 percent were vacant. Ford, Trinity Health, Livonia Public Schools and St. Mary Mercy Hospital rank among the largest employers. Newburgh and Nankin lakes lie in the south and southwest, Hines Drive links them, and the Rosedale Gardens Historic District and the Laurel Park Place mall at Six Mile and Newburgh roads are among the places buyers know. The median age at the 2020 census was 45.6, and many homes here have been owned for decades, so a long-held house often has a taxable value well below its market value, a gap that closes for the next owner after a sale.

Most Livonia homes sold with tax due close like any other: the title company gets a payoff, pays the city or county from the seller's proceeds, and records the deed. If the bill is delinquent, ask Wayne County for the payoff figure, since City Hall no longer holds the balance. Owners behind on taxes, with an inherited house or a place that needs work, can ask for a cash offer and have the payoff settled at the table.

September 14. The summer bill is mailed July 1, and if September 14 lands on a weekend or holiday the due date becomes the next business day.

Mail a check payable to the City of Livonia to Treasurer, 33000 Civic Center Drive, Livonia, MI 48154, or use the Treasurer's Office on the first floor of City Hall. Winter bills are due February 14.

Who do I call about a delinquent Livonia tax bill?

The Wayne County Treasurer. Delinquent real property taxes are turned over to the county, and the city's own records show current-year collections only.

How do I get the principal residence exemption in Livonia?

File the affidavit with the Assessment Department. Filing by June 1 covers that year's summer and winter taxes, and filing after June 1 through November 1 covers the winter levy.

Which school districts tax Livonia homes?

Livonia Public Schools serves most of the city, and a portion of the northeast is in Clarenceville Public Schools. Both appear among the bodies that receive the city's collections.

Whom do I deal with on a Kalamazoo tax bill?

City government divides the job in two. Values come from the Assessor, and bills come from the Treasurer. The assessor's counter at City Hall, 241 W South Street, is staffed Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call (269) 337-8000 or write assessor@kalamazoocity.org. The Assessor's page also lists two drop boxes open around the clock, one at the front of City Hall and a drive-up box on St. Johns Place at West Lovell Street.

Once the local collection window shuts, the Kalamazoo County Treasurer inherits the unpaid balance. Sellers get caught out at that handoff, because the county adds heavier charges than the city does.

Wikipedia counts 73,598 people in the 2020 census and calls Kalamazoo the county seat. Settlers arrived in 1829, the place was known as Bronson until 1836, and the city is home to Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo College and Kalamazoo Valley Community College.

When must Kalamazoo owners pay their taxes?

A year of tax comes as two bills. Summer notices are mailed by July 1 for payment by July 31, either in one sum or as six monthly installments that stay interest free while on time. Winter notices are mailed by December 1 for payment by the following February 14, in one sum.

By July 1Summer bills mailed

By December 1Winter bills mailed

The processor charges card users 2.8 percent with a $1.50 minimum and electronic check users $0.85, whether they pay online, by phone or in person.

How much extra does a late Kalamazoo bill cost?

Delinquent balances picked up by the County Treasurer carry a 4 percent administrative fee and monthly interest of 1 percent, plus costs for mailings, recording, title work and site visits. The county's sample schedule for 2025 taxes looks like this:

  • Local payment closes February 28; after that the county collects.
  • A $15 notice charge lands on October 1 of the next year.
  • The next March 1, a parcel over a year behind is forfeited and picks up half a percent monthly interest, 6 percent retroactive interest and a $175 title search charge.
  • Recording certificates adds $60, an in person site visit $50, and the newspaper listing $50.
  • Foreclosure follows at 25 months, with ownership passing to the County Treasurer on April 1.

Once the county owns the parcel, the owner cannot take it back. A person named on the deed may claim surplus money from an auction sale, and no treasurer can waive penalties or interest.

Can I delay or spread out my Kalamazoo tax?

Yes, in a few ways. A low income owner can request that the summer bill wait until the winter due date. Income for the preceding year must top out at $40,000, and the applicant must be 62 or older, the unmarried surviving spouse of such a person, blind, paraplegic, hemiplegic, quadriplegic, totally and permanently disabled, or an eligible veteran, service member, widow or widower. Applications reach the City Treasurer's Office by September 15, and no winter deferral exists.

After a bill reaches the county, the Treasurer can sign an extension agreement at an appointment with its foreclosure prevention team, reachable at 269-384-8124. The county expects two tax years to be cleared each calendar year, and dangerous or condemned buildings are not eligible.

Partial payments to the county are welcome because they slow the monthly interest. Staff there also check eligibility for the principal residence, poverty and disabled veteran exemptions.

How do I contest a Kalamazoo assessment?

Go first to the March Board of Review. MCL 211.30 sets its opening for the second Monday of March, with the city allowed to choose the Tuesday or Wednesday after. The board sits at least 12 hours that week, including 3 hours after 6 p.m.

When it agrees the value is off, it adjusts the assessed and taxable amounts to a fair level. You then receive written word of the outcome by the first Monday in June, with notice of the right to appeal further.

That next level is the Michigan Tax Tribunal, an independent tax court. Its Small Claims division hears most residential appeals in informal telephone sessions of about half an hour, and owners often appear without a lawyer. The board's notice gives the last day to file, so check it on arrival.

Which tax certificates does a Kalamazoo sale require?

A warranty deed needs two. In the city, the County Treasurer will not issue a certificate until the City Treasurer has issued one, for $10 at City Hall, 241 W South Street, phone 269-337-8036. The county certificate then costs $5 for up to 20 tax ID numbers. The state rule is MCL 211.135, which looks back five years from the deed date.

At the recording counter, 201 West Kalamazoo Avenue, the seller also owes transfer tax of $1.10 per $1,000 to the county and $7.50 per $1,000 to the state, after rounding the price up to the next $500. Applied to the city's Census median value of $179,000, that totals $1,539.40. The deed itself costs $30 to record.

Tax owed on the house is usually paid out of closing proceeds. Ask the treasurer holding the bill for the payoff, because city and county records are updated separately.

How does the home exemption change when I sell in Kalamazoo?

Owners who live in their home can claim the principal residence exemption, which removes a slice of the local school operating tax. Per the city, you must own and occupy the property by May 1 and file an affidavit with the Assessor.

Selling means new paperwork. The seller rescinds the exemption with the assessor, and the buyer files an affidavit of their own. Someone buying a replacement house can hold the old exemption for up to three years if the old house is vacant, listed, unleased and unused for business. The request is due May 1 following the exemption claim on the new house, and refiling by December 31 each year extends it for up to two more years.

Tell the closing agent when you moved out. A wrong exemption status on a sold house leads to corrected bills later.

What do Census figures say about Kalamazoo households?

Renters outnumber owners here, which is unusual for a Michigan city of this size. QuickFacts lists 72,683 residents in mid 2025 and 29,523 households, with owners in only 42.3 percent of homes.

  • Middle home value: $179,000.
  • Monthly gross rent, midpoint: $1,078.
  • Household income, midpoint: $52,272, with 24.9 percent of residents below the poverty line.
  • Land: 24.69 square miles, with about 2,980 residents on each.
  • Bachelor's degree or more, adults 25 and up: 38.5 percent.

Tenant occupied rentals, inherited houses and homes with deferred repairs often reach a sale with tax balances. The city's parcel lookup on BS&A Online displays tax history, payment dates, amounts due and permit history, so check yours before listing.

More questions about Kalamazoo, MI Property Tax Guide

What is the due date for a winter tax bill in Kalamazoo?

February 14 of the year after billing, paid in full. Anything open on March 1 moves to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer as delinquent.

Can a Kalamazoo owner split the summer bill into installments?

Yes, into six monthly payments, once the first installment arrives by July 31. A late first payment brings a single 3 percent penalty, and interest of 1 percent then accrues each month.

Who decides what my Kalamazoo house is assessed at?

The City Assessor's Office does. If you disagree, the March Board of Review hears you first, with the Michigan Tax Tribunal as the next step.

Who can defer a Kalamazoo summer bill?

Owners with prior year household income of $40,000 or under who are also 62 or older, blind, totally and permanently disabled, or a qualifying veteran, service member, widow or widower. The City Treasurer must receive the form by September 15.

How much are the tax certificates for a Kalamazoo warranty deed?

Ten dollars for the city certificate and five for the county one. A parcel inside the city needs both.

The city lies in Oakland County, and whatever the city has not collected by early March moves to the county treasurer. Once that happens the city cannot accept payment, so the address for your check changes along with the cost of lateness.

How is a Farmington Hills assessment set, and how do you challenge it?

The city aims for an assessed value equal to half of market value. Assessing studies 24 months of sales so that similar homes land in line, and each parcel is tied to a parcel number, a legal description and an address.

The State Tax Commission recommends reviewing roughly a fifth of properties each year, so an appraiser may stop by to look at your exterior. Notices of assessment go out every February, laying out the proposed valuation, the property class, principal residence exemption status, transfer status and appeal rights.

  • Call 248-871-2470 for an informal meeting with the assessor or staff before the March Board of Review.
  • Take a written appeal or an appointment request to the Board of Review in March.
  • Ask for copies of your records by phone or in person; broader requests go through the City Clerk as a records request.

The city recommends echecks, which post the same day with no fee. If one bounces, a $30 insufficient-funds charge follows.

  • In person at the Treasury counter during office hours.
  • A drive-up drop box in front of Police Headquarters, for checks only.
  • Mail to the city lockbox in Detroit, where payment counts when it is received, not when it is postmarked.

Confirm the parcel ID first, since sending money to the wrong property is the taxpayer's problem. A mailed payment needs the bill's top coupon and a check with your parcel number and phone number written on it. Do not mail after the due date.

The same page points owners to the Assessing Division for questions about the homestead exemption, hardship or veteran's exemptions and taxable value. The city also links a list of state property tax assistance programs.

What is Farmington Hills like for someone selling a house?

Farmington Hills covers 33.31 square miles in Oakland County, bordered by West Bloomfield to the north, Franklin and Southfield to the east, Livonia to the south and Novi to the west. The area began as the Quaker settlement of Quakertown after Arthur Power bought land in 1823, and Farmington Township was organized in 1827.

The economy runs on offices and engineering. Nissan's North American technical center, the United States headquarters of Bosch, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Beaumont Hospital, the city's largest employer in its 2019 financial report, are all in the city. Oakland Community College has its Orchard Ridge campus here.

Almost all of the city is in Farmington Public Schools, and small portions are in Clarenceville and Walled Lake Consolidated. The main roads are M-5, Orchard Lake Road, 12 Mile Road, I-696 and I-275, with SMART buses serving the area. The former Harrison High School building was reused as a community center called The Hawk.

What does a Farmington Hills seller owe at closing besides property tax?

The state transfer tax, $3.75 per $500 of value under MCL 207.525, lands on the grantor under MCL 207.523. At the QuickFacts median of $354,500 the math is 709 slices and $2,658.75, paid to the county treasurer inside 15 days of the deed being delivered.

A county transfer tax and recording fees come on top, and Oakland County's register sets its own charges. Before signing, ask the closing agent for a written statement showing the tax certificate, any open summer or winter balance and the recording costs.

  • A typical owned home is valued at $354,500, and owners occupy 64.7% of housing.
  • 35,529 households earn a median of $104,836.
  • Renters pay a median of $1,551 a month, and 57.6% of adults over 25 have a four-year degree.

These are citywide medians, and individual blocks will differ.

December 1 through February 16 without penalty. The bill is mailed November 30, and a 4% penalty is added on February 17.

At the Oakland County Treasurer, not the city. Per the city's page, taxes from 2025 and earlier have been turned over to the county at 1200 N Telegraph Road in Pontiac, phone 248-858-0611.

Is there a fee to pay Farmington Hills property tax by card?

Yes. Card payments add 2.8% plus $0.50. Echecks have no fee, though a returned one costs $30.

Call Assessing at 248-871-2470 for an informal meeting, then use the March Board of Review, either by appointment or by letter received before the last meeting day.

Possibly. The city's deferment form for 2026 covered owners 62 or older, or disabled, blind or a qualifying veteran or surviving spouse, with 2025 household income under $40,000. Ask Treasury for the current form.

Novi by the numbers

Which Novi offices send and collect the property tax bill?

Novi's own Treasurer's Office mails and collects the bills, while the city Assessing Department supplies the values behind them. The treasurer works from 45175 Ten Mile Road, Novi, MI 48375, and answers tax questions at 248-347-0440. The Treasurer page also links the online property and tax search.

Novi sits in Oakland County, about 25 miles northwest of downtown Detroit, and covers roughly 30 square miles of land around Walled Lake. I-96, I-696, I-275 and M-5 all reach the city, and the population rose from about 9,700 in 1970 to 66,243 in 2020. Novi became a city in 1969, after starting life as a township in 1832.

The city is only the collecting agent for most of what appears on the statement. Its own operating taxes are billed in full on the summer statement, while the winter statement carries the county, school and authority levies. Novi has no say over the county and school rates.

When are Novi property taxes due?

Two payment seasons apply: late summer and winter. The city's 2026 notice said summer bills would be mailed the week of July 1 and that payments had to reach the treasurer on or before August 31 to avoid an automatic penalty. For anyone reading after that date, the winter window is the one to watch.

A drop box sits behind the Civic Center, and the 2026 notice accepted drop box payments until midnight on the deadline day. Online payment by credit card or electronic check is available through cityofnovi.org. Be careful with the bank numbers you type, because a returned payment after the due date draws the penalty.

How does Novi set the taxable value of a house?

The bill rests on taxable value, a figure that normally sits below half of what the house would fetch. The assessor estimates market value as of Tax Day, December 31 of the year before, and the assessed value is about 50% of that. For 2026 the city used a 24-month sales study running from April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2025, covering roughly 2,000 sales.

Taxable value grows more slowly than assessed value. The 2026 inflation rate multiplier is 1.027, so a home that stays with its owner can rise no more than 2.7%, even if neighborhood prices climbed 10%. The city's formula is the prior taxable value, less losses, times the multiplier, plus additions.

  • Taxable value is the lesser of assessed value and capped value.
  • The tax equals taxable value divided by 1,000, times the millage rate.
  • A sale resets the taxable value to the assessed value the following year.
  • Special assessments, trash charges and penalties are added on top.

After you sell, the next owner's bill will probably run higher than yours did. Tell any buyer to look at the assessed value rather than your old bill.

What is the process to appeal a Novi assessment?

Appeals start with the March Board of Review, the sole yearly chance to contest a current value. Hearings begin on the second Monday of March, after the Notice of Assessment goes out in mid February. Petition forms come from the Assessing Department or the city's website, and you make an appointment to appear.

If the board's answer is not acceptable, the next level is the Michigan Tax Tribunal. A residential petition must go to the Tribunal at 611 W. Ottawa St., Lansing, MI 48933 by July 31, and only after you have appeared before the March board. Commercial and industrial appeals to the Tribunal are due May 31. The July and December boards cannot hear value disputes under MCL 211.53b.

Two relief options sit outside the appeal process. Michigan has no age-based property tax break, but Novi offers an annual poverty exemption based on income and assets, which needs Board of Review approval. Owners who qualify can also ask the Treasurer's Office about deferring summer taxes.

What is a Novi tax bill spent on?

On the city's sample winter statement, about 59% of a homestead bill went to education, 30% to the City of Novi and 11% to Oakland County. That split was based on the Novi and OCC district homestead rates, so a parcel in another district will differ. Several school systems reach into the city.

  • Novi Community Schools cover most of the city.
  • Northville Public Schools serve a large part of the south side.
  • Walled Lake Consolidated Schools take in a pocket with two elementary schools.
  • South Lyon Community Schools hold a small western strip.

The statement's other lines include the county parks and recreation levy, the zoo authority, the art institute, Oakland transit and the Huron Clinton Metropolitan Authority. Check the parcel number and school district code on your own bill before you compare it with a neighbor's.

What do federal housing counts show for Novi?

Census QuickFacts lists 67,319 people in Novi for July 2025 and 26,801 households across 2020 to 2024. Owners live in 66.3% of housing units. The typical owned home is valued at $421,900, rent at the middle is $1,747 a month, and household income at the middle is $110,723.

A condo near the I-96 corridor and a lakeside house will sit well apart from those citywide figures. About 29% of residents were born abroad. Health care, automotive suppliers and the retail cluster around Novi Road and I-96 anchor the local economy.

What follows when Novi tax goes unpaid?

After the winter period closes, the balance moves to Oakland County. MCL 211.78a returns taxes still owed on March 1 as delinquent, adding a 4% county fee and interest at 1% for each month. The county treasurer collects from there, and ongoing nonpayment leads into a three-year foreclosure process.

For 2024 and earlier balances, the county's notices name March 31, 2027 as the final day to pay and keep the property. The treasurer's office, at 248-858-0611, offers repayment schedules and referrals. Our Oakland County property tax guide lays out the foreclosure calendar step by step.

What should a Novi seller do about the principal residence exemption?

The exemption takes up to 18 mills of school operating tax off a home you own and occupy. To see it on the summer bill, you had to be both owner and resident by June 1. People who moved in between June 2 and November 1 can claim a winter exemption.

On a sale, send the Assessing Department the rescission form so the exemption ends on the correct date. A seller who has already bought another Michigan residence may keep it on the old house through a conditional rescission, as long as the old house is listed, vacant, unleased and free of business use. Submit that form with the new exemption by June 1 for both bills, or by November 1 for winter only.

How does a Novi sale handle the tax bill?

At closing, the title company splits the current year's tax between seller and buyer and settles any unpaid amount out of your proceeds. Get the present balance from the city treasurer. If any year has moved to Oakland County, buy an official delinquent tax statement through the county's Property Gateway, which sells them to owners and title companies.

A sale can close with tax owing, since the payoff is a line on the seller's settlement statement. The avoidable cost is the late charge: miss the winter deadline and a 3% penalty applies that staff cannot waive. Pay early, and keep both statements for the year of the sale.

When is the winter tax deadline in Novi?

February 14. The winter statement allows payment from December 1 through February 14, and the money has to be physically in the treasurer's hands by that day. A 3% penalty starts after it, and no one at the counter can waive it.

Will a postmark count as on-time in Novi?

No. The city's notices say postmarks and post-dated checks are refused. Use the drop box behind the Civic Center, pay online, or mail the check early enough to arrive on time.

Do taxes rise after buying a Novi house?

Often. The year after a sale, taxable value resets to the assessed value, which may sit well above the earlier capped figure. Later increases are limited to the inflation multiplier or 5%, whichever is smaller.

Which Novi department answers questions about my value?

The Assessing Department handles values, exemptions, and name or address changes. Bills and payments go through the Treasurer's Office at 248-347-0440.

Yes. The title company pays the balance, with penalty and interest, from your proceeds at closing. Request a current statement first from the city, or from the Oakland County Treasurer for earlier years.

Rochester Hills sits in Oakland County, about 25 miles north of downtown Detroit, so most owners deal with a city office first and the county office only if a bill goes delinquent.

Local schools, Oakland Community College, the Oakland Schools intermediate district, the county, county parks, the Detroit Zoo, the Art Institute and Oakland Transit all take a share. The city's own portion pays for roads, fire, the library, the OPC Social and Activity Center and the Rochester Avon Recreation Authority. When are Rochester Hills property taxes due?

Two bills arrive each year, a summer bill and a winter bill, and each has a payment window that closes in mid-September or mid-February. The summer bill covers school and county taxes only, so the city's own levies fall on the winter bill.

The city does not honor postmarks. A check dropped in the mail on the due date counts as late, so use the black drop box at City Hall, pay online or walk it in. Online payment by e-check carries no fee, and cards carry a 2.75% processing fee and never less than $1.50. First State Bank also takes cash or check, but you must hand over the whole tax bill. Enrollment in recurring automatic payment, which draws on a bank account, costs nothing.

How can an owner lower or delay the tax bill?

Rochester Hills offers a summer tax deferment for owners with limited income. The city form tied to a 2025 deadline set the household income ceiling at $40,000 and listed these groups:

  • Owners aged 62 or older, including an unremarried surviving spouse.
  • Paraplegic or quadriplegic owners.
  • Eligible service members, veterans and widows.
  • Blind owners.
  • Totally and permanently disabled owners.

Applicants file the city form together with a copy of their Michigan Homestead Property Tax Credit claim. The filing date moves each year, so ask Treasury for the current form and deadline. Disabled veterans can also ask about the exemption in MCL 211.7b, which the city links from both its tax and deferment pages.

For the amount of the bill itself, the lever is the assessment. The Assessing Department mails notices in February, and a homeowner who finds the value too steep books an appointment before the Board of Review in March. Under state law the board convenes in the second week of March, and the board must send each protester a written decision, with Michigan Tax Tribunal appeal details, ahead of the first Monday of June (MCL 211.30).

What happens to the taxable value when a Rochester Hills house sells?

The buyer's taxable value resets to the state equalized value the year after the sale. Until then, taxable value climbs each year by no more than the smaller of 5% or inflation, and it can never exceed the state equalized value (MCL 211.27a). A seller who has lived in the house for many years may have a much lower bill than the buyer will, and the difference is worth knowing before a listing goes up.

The city's assessing FAQ gives owners a rough way to forecast a bill: take half of the estimated property value and multiply by the current millage rate. For an addition, it suggests treating half the project cost as added taxable value. Its example is a $30,000 project, which adds $15,000 of taxable value before the millage is applied.

After closing, the buyer should receive a Property Transfer Affidavit and a Principal Residence Exemption affidavit from the closing agent. Both go to the Assessors Office at City Hall, staffed on weekdays from morning to late afternoon. State law gives the buyer 45 days from the transfer to report it to the assessor.

What should a seller know about the city itself?

Rochester Hills became a city in 1984, when Avon Township voters approved a charter and chose the name over the alternative, Avon Hills. Its 32.9 square miles are almost entirely land, bounded by Troy to the south, Auburn Hills to the west, Shelby Township in Macomb County to the east and Oakland Township to the north. The 2020 census counted 76,300 residents and 31,208 housing units, of which 4.8% stood vacant.

Rochester Community Schools covers the larger share of the city and operates Rochester Adams, Rochester and Stoney Creek high schools. Avondale School District covers some of the rest, and the district printed on the bill sets the school millage. Oakland University and Rochester Christian University also have programs in the city.

A seller behind on taxes has a practical path. Ask Treasury for the exact balance and the penalty clock, get a payoff statement from the title agent, and have the unpaid amount paid off through the closing statement. If the bill has already gone to Oakland County, call the county treasurer at 248-858-0611, since the city bill carries a notice pointing owners to county hardship help.

What does the county take over after March 1?

Any balance still open on March 2 belongs to Oakland County, not the city, and the city's pay options no longer apply. Tax bills carry a notice if prior year taxes were returned delinquent, pointing the owner to the county treasurer's hardship line. Interest and penalties keep growing, so anyone selling a parcel with delinquent tax should clear it before listing or build the payoff into the closing statement.

For a deed with warranty covenants, state law has the register of deeds ask for a county treasurer certificate that no tax liens exist and that taxes for the five preceding years are paid (MCL 211.135). A quitclaim deed with no warranty is excepted from that rule. Either way, a clean tax history keeps a sale moving.

Which number reaches the Rochester Hills assessor?

Dial 248-656-4605 for the Assessing Department. It handles values, name and address changes, and the Principal Residence Exemption. The office is at 1000 Rochester Hills Drive, inside City Hall.

What is the penalty if I miss the Rochester Hills summer deadline?

Interest of 1% attaches the day after the deadline and a further 1% attaches each month after that. The city also adds a 3% penalty after the mid-February winter deadline. Postmarks are not honored.

Does a sale change the next tax bill?

Yes. A transfer of ownership resets the taxable value to the state equalized value for the year after the sale. A buyer who inherits a long-held house can see a noticeably higher bill than the seller paid.

Can I pay my Rochester Hills tax bill by card?

Yes, online, by phone or at the Treasurer's office, with a 2.75% processing fee and a $1.50 minimum. E-check online is free. Checks go in the drop box at City Hall or by mail.

Where do delinquent Rochester Hills taxes go?

They go to the Oakland County Treasurer, 1200 N. Telegraph, Pontiac, MI 48341, from March 2. The county treasurer's number printed on the bill is 248-858-0611.
